text: Two JavaScript features trip up more ServiceNow developers than almost anything else: how var, let, and const actually scope a variable, and how the this keyword behaves differently inside a callback. This lesson covers both, with the real bug pattern you'll actually run into on the job, and the standard fix for each.

A var declared inside an if block is still visible throughout the whole function - that's function scope, and it's also hoisted, so referencing it before its line just returns undefined instead of throwing a real error. In this example, a var declared inside the if block leaks out and is still readable afterward, which is rarely what the developer intended. A let declared in that same spot would not exist at all outside the block - referencing it early, or outside the block, throws instead of quietly returning undefined.

Here's the real bug. A regular function passed to forEach gets called by forEach itself, not by the object that owns the outer method. So inside that callback, this does not refer to the outer object the way you'd expect - it points somewhere else entirely, and a property like this.label comes back undefined.

The fix is switching that inner function to an arrow function. An arrow function has no this of its own - it inherits this lexically from the scope where it was written. Nothing else in the code changes, and now this inside the callback correctly refers to the outer object again.

At a glance: var is function-scoped and hoisted and can leak out of a block; let and const are block-scoped and aren't usable before their declaration line; and an arrow function's this is inherited from the enclosing scope rather than decided by how it's called.
Next up, string and date handling - the native string methods you already know, plus the real reason ServiceNow has its own GlideDateTime object instead of just using JavaScript's built-in Date.
